title: Secure Data and Model Deployment Pipelines (MLOps/LLMOps)
intro: Securing the machinery that turns data into deployed models: hardened CI/CD with pinned inputs, minimal containers and signed provenance; integrity and confidentiality through ingestion and transformation; automatic lineage for fine-tuned models; validation checkpoints and gates that can’t be bypassed; and unlearning built in as an engineering capability.
objectives: Secure CI/CD for models: ephemeral runners, federated credentials, pinned inputs, minimal signed containers and safe model packaging
Apply integrity and confidentiality controls through data ingestion and transformation zones
Capture lineage for fine-tuning automatically, and use it for incident response, erasure, licensing and rollback
Place validation checkpoints along the pipeline and make gates enforceable with attestations, policy as code and separation of duties
Build unlearning into MLOps through lineage, deletion workflows, suitable methods, verification and design for forgetting

sections.title: Secure CI/CD for models: packaging and containers

blocks.title: The pipeline is part of the product

scenes.title: The pipeline is part of the product
scenes.sub: Securing CI/CD, packaging and containers for models
scenes.say: Whoever controls your pipeline controls what your users run. If an attacker can change a build step, they never need to touch production. | This video covers securing the continuous integration and delivery pipelines that build, package and ship models.

scenes.title: How pipelines get compromised

items.d: One build can tamper with the next

scenes.say: Pipelines are compromised in predictable ways, which OWASP catalogues in its top ten risks for CI and CD. | Poisoned pipeline execution: an untrusted change, such as a pull request from a fork, runs pipeline steps that can reach secrets. | Leaked credentials: long-lived cloud keys stored in pipeline settings. | Unpinned dependencies, so each build pulls whatever happens to be latest. | Shared, persistent build runners, where one build can tamper with the next. | Weak flow control, where changes reach production without review. | And bloated base images, especially for GPU workloads, carrying hundreds of packages nobody needs.

scenes.title: A hardened model build
scenes.say: Here is a hardened build for a model service. It starts from reviewed source, on protected branches, including the pipeline definition itself. | The build runs on an ephemeral runner: isolated, created fresh for each build, and destroyed afterwards. | Every input is pinned: dependencies by hash from internal mirrors, base images by digest, and model weights by content hash. | The output is a minimal container image that runs as non-root and is scanned for vulnerabilities. | The build produces a software bill of materials and a signed provenance attestation describing exactly how it was built. | And the signed artefacts go to an immutable registry, where deployment gates verify them.

scenes.title: Packaging a model for deployment
scenes.say: There are two common ways to package a model with its serving code. | Bake the weights into the container image, or have the image fetch the weights from a model registry when it starts. | Baking in gives one signed, immutable unit, so what was tested is exactly what runs. Pulling at start keeps images small, and makes swapping models easy. | But baked images can be enormous and slow to roll out, while pulled weights must be verified, by signature and hash, before the server loads them.

scenes.title: Pipeline controls that matter most
scenes.say: Five controls matter most. | Use federated, short-lived credentials, where the pipeline proves its identity to the cloud, instead of stored cloud keys. | Treat the pipeline definition as code that needs review, with named owners for pipeline files. | Never give untrusted changes access to secrets: builds from forks or unreviewed branches run without them. | Pin and verify every input, through lockfiles, image digests and model hashes. | And sign and attest every output, so deployment can verify what it is about to run.

items: Pipelines are attack surface: protect them like production
Ephemeral runners, pinned inputs, minimal images
Federated credentials; no secrets for untrusted changes
SBOMs, signed provenance and an immutable registry
scenes.say: To recap. | Pipelines are attack surface, so protect them like production. | Build on ephemeral runners with pinned inputs, producing minimal images. | Use federated, short-lived credentials, and never expose secrets to untrusted changes. | And publish software bills of materials, signed provenance and immutable artefacts for deployment to verify.

blocks.md:
### Threats to ML pipelines
The OWASP **Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks** list applies directly to MLOps. The most relevant are insufficient flow control (changes reaching production without review), inadequate identity and access management, dependency chain abuse, **poisoned pipeline execution** (untrusted code running inside the pipeline with its privileges), insufficient credential hygiene, insecure system configuration, and ungoverned use of third-party services. ML pipelines add model weights, datasets and very large GPU base images to the list of inputs that can be tampered with.

### Build integrity
- **SLSA** (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines build levels: provenance exists (level 1); a hosted build platform generates signed provenance (level 2); and a hardened platform isolates builds from each other and protects the signing material, so provenance can’t be forged (level 3).
- **Ephemeral, isolated runners**, created per build, prevent one job from poisoning another; avoid self-hosted runners on persistent machines for untrusted code.
- **Pinned inputs:** lockfiles with hashes, base images by digest rather than tag, internal package mirrors (Module 3.7), and model weights and datasets referenced by content hash.
- **Reproducible builds**, where practical, let anyone confirm that an artefact came from the stated source.

### Credentials and secrets
- **Workload identity federation** (OpenID Connect between the CI platform and the cloud) issues short-lived credentials scoped to a specific repository, branch and environment, replacing stored keys.
- **Separate credentials per stage and environment** (Module 3.5), with production deployment needing approval.
- **Never** run untrusted pull requests with access to secrets or privileged runners.
- Scan repositories and build logs for leaked secrets.

### Containers for model serving
- Start from **minimal or distroless base images**; GPU images built on large vendor bases often carry many vulnerabilities, so choose slim variants and patch regularly.
- **Multi-stage builds** keep compilers and build tools out of the final image; never copy secrets into layers.
- Run as **non-root**, with a read-only file system where possible and only the capabilities needed.
- Generate an **SBOM** (and an AIBOM for model components), scan for vulnerabilities, and **sign images** (for example, with Sigstore cosign).
- Enforce at deployment with **admission control**: only signed images, from approved registries, meeting policy.

### Packaging the model
Use safe weight formats (safetensors), package the tokenizer and configuration alongside the weights, and record everything in a signed manifest (Module 3.6). Whether weights are baked into the image or pulled at start-up, deployment must verify them against the registry before loading.

blocks.title: CI/CD questions
blocks.md: Look for answers that remove **standing secrets** (federated, short-lived credentials), stop **untrusted code reaching privileged steps**, and make outputs **verifiable** (pinned inputs, SBOMs, signed provenance). Scanning alone is weaker than preventing tampering in the first place.

q.q: A team’s model-training pipeline runs automatically on every pull request, including those from external forks, using a runner that holds cloud credentials for the training cluster. What is the MAIN risk?
o: Builds will run slowly, because every single pull request starts a full training job on the cluster
An attacker can submit a pull request whose code runs with the pipeline’s cloud credentials
The training cluster’s GPUs will overheat from running too many jobs at once
Reviewers will struggle to read all of the build logs produced by each run
q.why: This is poisoned pipeline execution: untrusted code from a fork runs inside the pipeline with access to its secrets. Untrusted changes must run without credentials, on isolated runners, with privileged steps only after review.

scenes.title: Clean data, kept clean
scenes.sub: Integrity and confidentiality in ingestion and transformation
scenes.say: Between the raw sources and the training set sits a chain of ingestion and transformation jobs. Each one can corrupt the data, leak it, or quietly let poisoned records through. | This video covers integrity and confidentiality controls for data ingestion and transformation pipelines.

scenes.title: Zones in a data pipeline
scenes.say: Good pipelines move data through zones, each with its own controls. Data arrives from internal and external sources. | New data lands in quarantine first, where it is validated against its schema, scanned for malware, personal data and secrets, and checked against expected hashes. | Data that passes is written to an immutable raw zone: append-only and versioned, so the original can always be recovered and compared. | Transformation jobs, running reviewed and tested code, clean, join and enrich the data into a curated zone, handling personal data as policy requires. | And the training set is a pinned, hashed snapshot of curated data, so every model can be traced to exactly what it learned from.

scenes.title: Integrity controls

items.d: Detect changes in transit or at rest

scenes.say: Integrity controls stop data being corrupted, accidentally or deliberately. | Data contracts define agreed schemas, value ranges and owners for each feed. | Checksums for every batch detect changes in transit or at rest. | Immutable, versioned storage keeps an append-only raw zone that can’t be quietly rewritten. | Transformations are code: reviewed, tested and versioned, never edited by hand in production. | Distribution checks spot sudden shifts, outliers and unusual label changes, which can signal poisoning. | And every write is audited: who changed what, and when.

scenes.title: Confidentiality controls

items.d: In transit and at rest, managed keys
Each job reads only what it needs

scenes.say: Confidentiality controls stop the data leaking along the way. | Encrypt data in transit and at rest, with managed keys. | Give each job least privilege, reading only the data it needs, with its own identity. | Protect personal data early, tokenising or pseudonymising identifiers at ingestion, so later stages never see raw values. | Apply column- and row-level security in curated data. | Keep environments separate, with no production data in development unless it is masked or synthetic. | And clean up intermediate files and temporary copies, which are a common source of forgotten sensitive data.

items: Quarantine, then immutable raw, then curated, then pinned snapshots
Contracts, checksums, versioning and audited writes protect integrity
Encryption, least privilege and early PII protection keep data confidential
Distribution checks catch poisoning before training
scenes.say: To recap. | Move data from quarantine, to an immutable raw zone, to curated data, to pinned training snapshots. | Protect integrity with data contracts, checksums, versioning and audited writes. | Keep data confidential with encryption, least-privilege jobs and early protection of personal data. | And use distribution checks to catch poisoning before it reaches training.

blocks.md:
### Pipeline zones
Many data platforms use a layered **"medallion"** pattern: **bronze** (raw, as ingested), **silver** (cleaned and conformed) and **gold** (curated for specific uses). Adding a **quarantine** zone in front of bronze, and treating bronze as immutable, gives a strong security structure:

| Zone | Purpose | Key controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Quarantine** | Hold new data until it passes checks | Schema validation, malware and secret scanning, PII detection, hash verification, source authentication |
| **Raw (bronze)** | Faithful, recoverable copy of what arrived | Append-only or object lock, versioning, encryption, restricted write access |
| **Curated (silver and gold)** | Cleaned, joined, enriched data | Transformations as reviewed code, data quality tests, column- and row-level security, lineage capture |
| **Training snapshots** | Exactly what a model learns from | Content hashes, immutable storage, links to the training run (Section 3) |

### Integrity
- **Data contracts** between producers and consumers specify schema, semantics, quality thresholds, owners and change processes; break the pipeline, rather than silently accept, when a contract is violated.
- **Checksums and signed manifests** for batches and files detect corruption and tampering between stages.
- **Versioned, immutable storage** (object lock, table formats with time travel, data version control tools) lets you prove what data looked like at any time, and roll back.
- **Data quality and distribution tests** (ranges, null rates, duplicates, label balance, outliers, near-duplicate clusters) catch both errors and poisoning attempts (Module 3.3).
- **Transformations as code**, through the same review and CI process as application code; no manual edits in production.
- **Audit logs** for writes, deletes and permission changes.

### Confidentiality
- Encryption in transit and at rest with managed keys (Module 3.4); private endpoints between pipeline components.
- **Per-job identities** with least privilege; no shared "data platform" super-account.
- **Early PII handling:** detect and tokenise or pseudonymise at ingestion; keep re-identification keys separately (Module 3.2).
- **Fine-grained access** in curated layers: column masking, row-level filters and purpose-based policies (Module 3.4).
- **Environment separation** and masked or synthetic data for development and testing.
- **Lifecycle management:** expire temporary tables, caches and exports; include them in retention schedules.

### Reproducibility as a security property
If you can re-run a transformation from a pinned raw snapshot and get identical output, you can detect tampering, investigate incidents and prove to auditors exactly how training data was produced (Module 3.1).

blocks.title: Ingestion questions
blocks.md: Favour designs where data is **validated before it is trusted** (quarantine), the original is **immutable and versioned**, and every transformation is **reviewed code with audit trails**. For confidentiality, protecting personal data **as early as possible** beats trying to protect it everywhere later.

blocks.title: Match the control to the zone
pairs: A content hash linked to the training run

q.q: A pipeline lets analysts correct records directly in the raw data zone when they spot errors, overwriting the original files. What is the MAIN problem with this?
o: It makes the raw zone’s storage costs grow much faster than the costs of the pipeline’s other zones
Originals are lost, so tampering can’t be detected and changes can’t be traced or reversed
It means analysts must have training in the data platform’s query language
It slows down training, because corrected files must be downloaded again
q.why: An immutable, versioned raw zone preserves what actually arrived, so corruption or poisoning can be detected, investigated and rolled back. Corrections belong in reviewed transformations that produce new versions, with audit trails.

scenes.title: Every fine-tune has ancestors
scenes.say: A fine-tuned model is built from a base model, several datasets, some code and a set of choices, and it may itself become the parent of further models. When something goes wrong, you need that family tree. | This video covers lineage tracking for fine-tuning: what to record, how to capture it, and what it lets you do.

scenes.title: A fine-tuned model’s family tree
scenes.say: Here is a fine-tuned model’s family tree. It starts with a base model, recorded by exact version and hash. | Then the datasets used for tuning, each recorded as a snapshot with its own content hash, including any synthetic or preference data. | The fine-tuning run ties them together, recording the code commit, hyperparameters, container image and who launched it. | The run produces an adapter, such as a set of LoRA weights, or a fully tuned model. | It also produces evaluation results, linked to the approval decision. | And finally a deployed version in the registry, which can be traced back through every one of these links.

scenes.title: What lineage lets you answer

items.h: Which models used a bad dataset?
What do we roll back to?

scenes.say: Lineage turns hard questions into simple queries. | If a dataset turns out to be poisoned or contaminated, which models, adapters and deployments used it? | If someone asks for erasure, which models were trained on their data? | Which licence terms from the base model and data flow down to this model? | Can we rebuild this model exactly, for an auditor or an investigation? | If a version misbehaves, what is the last good ancestor to roll back to? | And what must go into technical documentation, for example under the EU AI Act?

scenes.title: Manual records and automatic capture
scenes.say: Lineage only works if it is complete. | Manual records live in spreadsheets and notes, while automatic capture means the pipeline records every run as it happens. | Manual records develop gaps, typos and drift. Automatic capture is complete and consistent. | And manual effort is high and never ends, while automatic capture is built once into the pipeline and then costs almost nothing.

items: Record base model, data snapshots, code, settings, environment and launcher
Link runs to adapters, evaluations, approvals and deployments
Lineage answers poisoning, erasure, licensing, rebuild and rollback questions
Capture it automatically in the pipeline, not by hand
scenes.say: To recap. | Record the base model, data snapshots, code, settings, environment and who launched each fine-tuning run. | Link each run to its adapters, evaluations, approvals and deployments. | Lineage answers questions about poisoning, erasure, licensing, rebuilding and rollback. | And capture it automatically in the pipeline, never by hand.

blocks.md:
### What to record for each fine-tuning run
| Element | Details to capture |
|---|---|
| **Base model** | Publisher, name, exact version, content hash, licence, source registry |
| **Data** | Dataset IDs and snapshot hashes for training, validation and test sets; filters and transformations applied; synthetic data and the model that generated it; preference or feedback data |
| **Code and configuration** | Repository commit, training script version, hyperparameters, random seeds, tokenizer version |
| **Environment** | Container image digest, library versions, hardware type |
| **Run metadata** | Run ID, start and end time, who or what launched it, approvals obtained |
| **Outputs** | Adapter or model hashes, checkpoints, evaluation results, model card updates |
| **Downstream links** | Merges with other models, adapters stacked on it, distilled models, deployments and the systems using them |

### Fine-tuning complicates lineage
- **Chains:** models are fine-tuned from already fine-tuned models, so lineage must be a graph that can be traversed through many generations.
- **Adapters:** LoRA and similar adapters are small files that may be combined with different base models; record each adapter’s base model and compatible versions.
- **Merges:** model merging combines several parents; record every parent and the merge method.
- **Synthetic and distilled data:** data generated by another model inherits that model’s licence terms and flaws, so record the generator.
- **Third-party fine-tuning services:** keep the provider’s job IDs, model versions and data retention terms in your records.

### Capturing lineage
Use the pipeline and platform to capture lineage automatically: experiment-tracking and model-registry tools record runs, parameters and artefacts; open standards such as **OpenLineage** describe data jobs; and **AIBOMs** (for example, CycloneDX’s machine learning bill of materials) describe a model’s components for sharing (Module 2.5). Make lineage records **immutable** and link them to signed artefacts (Module 3.6).

### Using lineage
- **Incident response:** when a dataset is found to be poisoned, query every model, adapter and deployment that descends from it (Domain 5).
- **Privacy requests:** identify every model trained on a person’s data, as the starting point for unlearning (Section 5).
- **Licensing:** trace the terms that apply to a deployed model through its base model and data.
- **Compliance:** the EU AI Act’s technical documentation for high-risk systems (Annex IV) expects a description of data, training methods and changes over the lifecycle.
- **Rollback:** identify the last known good ancestor (Module 3.5).

blocks.title: Lineage questions
blocks.md: When a question asks how to find **which models are affected** by a bad dataset, a leaked record or a licence problem, the answer is **lineage tracking** linked to the model registry and AIBOMs. The strongest options capture lineage **automatically** and immutably as part of the pipeline.

q.q: Six months after release, a dataset used in several fine-tuning runs is found to contain poisoned records. What MOST quickly identifies every affected model and deployment?
o: Asking each data science team to recall which datasets they used in recent projects
Querying automatically captured lineage that links datasets, runs, models and deployments
Re-running evaluations on every model in production, looking for any sign of unusual behaviour
Searching shared drives for spreadsheets that mention the dataset’s name
q.why: Automatically captured, linked lineage turns the question into a query across generations of models. Memory and spreadsheets are incomplete, and re-evaluation may miss poisoning designed to stay hidden.

scenes.title: Gates that can’t be skipped
scenes.sub: Validation checkpoints and pipeline gating patterns
scenes.say: A gate is only a control if it can’t be skipped. Many pipelines have checks that are optional, advisory, or easy to bypass under deadline pressure. | This video covers where to put validation checkpoints in an ML pipeline, and the patterns that make gates enforceable.

scenes.title: Checkpoints along the pipeline
scenes.say: Checkpoints belong at six points. | At ingestion: data must meet its contract and pass scans and hash checks. | Before training: the data must be approved for this purpose, with licences and lawful basis confirmed. | After training: performance, safety and fairness evaluations against agreed thresholds. | A security checkpoint: artefact scanning, dependency checks and, for higher tiers, red-team results. | A release checkpoint: approval by the right authority for the model’s risk tier. | And a canary checkpoint: live metrics must stay within limits before the rollout widens.

scenes.title: Kinds of gate
rows: Only as good as its tests
scenes.say: Gates come in three kinds, and good pipelines use all three. | Automated gates decide by thresholds and tests. Human gates use judgement and context. Policy-as-code gates check machine-readable rules, such as only deploying signed models approved for this tier. | Automated gates suit every build, because they are fast. Human gates suit high-risk releases. Policy as code gives consistent enforcement everywhere. | But automated gates are only as good as their tests, human gates are slow and prone to rubber-stamping, and policy rules need maintaining as things change.

scenes.title: Making gates enforceable
scenes.say: Six patterns make gates enforceable. | Each gate produces signed evidence of its result: an attestation. | Deployment verifies the attestations, and refuses anything missing one, so gates can’t be skipped by going around the pipeline. | The pipeline itself is protected, so required checks can’t simply be removed by whoever is in a hurry. | Duties are separated: the people who build a model don’t approve it. | Emergencies use a controlled break-glass route: approved, logged, and expiring, with review afterwards. | And gate health is tracked: overrides, failures and flaky tests are signals that controls are eroding.

items: Checkpoints at ingest, pre-train, post-train, security, release and canary
Combine automated, human and policy-as-code gates
Attest each gate; verify attestations at deployment
Protect pipeline config, separate duties, control break-glass
scenes.say: To recap. | Place checkpoints at ingestion, before training, after training, for security, at release and during canary. | Combine automated, human and policy-as-code gates. | Make each gate produce a signed attestation, and verify the attestations at deployment. | And protect the pipeline configuration, separate duties, and keep break-glass routes controlled and reviewed.

blocks.md:
### Checkpoints and their evidence
| Checkpoint | Typical checks | Evidence produced |
|---|---|---|
| **Ingestion** | Schema and contract, malware and secret scans, PII detection, hash verification | Validation report; dataset version and hash |
| **Pre-training** | Data approved for the purpose (licence, lawful basis, classification), dataset pinned | Data approval record linked to the run |
| **Post-training evaluation** | Performance against baseline, safety and robustness suites, fairness metrics, memorisation tests | Evaluation report with thresholds and results |
| **Security** | Artefact format and malware scanning, dependency and container scans, signature checks, red teaming for higher tiers | Scan results, red-team findings and remediation status |
| **Release approval** | Evidence complete for the risk tier; approver independent of the builders (Module 3.5) | Signed approval in the registry |
| **Canary and rollout** | Error rates, safety signals, drift and business metrics within limits (Module 3.5) | Automated promotion or rollback decision |

### Gate design
- **Hard and soft gates:** hard gates block on failure; soft gates warn and require acknowledgement. Make security, privacy and safety gates hard for higher risk tiers.
- **Thresholds agreed in advance**, recorded with the model’s approval, so they can’t be adjusted after a failure to let a release through.
- **Policy as code:** express rules (for example "production accepts only signed models with an approved evaluation attestation for their tier") in a policy engine such as Open Policy Agent, and enforce them in the pipeline and at admission to the serving platform.
- **Attestations:** each gate records a signed statement of what was checked and the result (for example, in-toto attestations), bound to the artefact’s digest. The deployment step verifies the full set.

### Preventing bypass
- **Branch protection and required checks** on the pipeline repository; pipeline definitions changed only through review.
- **Deployment only from the pipeline:** no human credentials can deploy to production directly.
- **Separation of duties:** the person or team that builds a model can’t approve or deploy it alone.
- **Break-glass procedures** for emergencies: a named approver, time-limited access, full logging, and mandatory review afterwards.
- **Monitor gate metrics:** frequent overrides, waivers or "temporarily disabled" checks are early warning signs.

Module 4.4 covers functional, performance and stress testing, which supply many of the automated gates; Module 6.2 covers secure AI development lifecycle and change management.

blocks.title: Gating questions
blocks.md: The best answers make gates **mandatory and verifiable**: signed evidence bound to the artefact, checked at deployment, with separation of duties. Answers that rely on teams "remembering" to run checks, or that let thresholds change after a failure, are weak.

blocks.title: Which checkpoint catches this?
pairs: A dataset arrives with an unexpected column
A fairness gap exceeds the agreed threshold
A checkpoint uses an unsafe file format
Errors rise for the 5% of users on the new version

q.q: Under deadline pressure, an engineer deploys a model directly from a laptop, skipping the pipeline’s evaluation and security gates. Which control MOST directly prevents this?
o: A policy reminding engineers that every deployment must go through the pipeline, with no exceptions
Accepting only artefacts with valid gate attestations, deployed by the pipeline’s identity
A monthly report listing every deployment that didn’t go through the pipeline
Extra training for engineers on why the evaluation gates are important
q.why: If production only accepts artefacts carrying signed attestations from each gate, deployed by the pipeline’s own identity, bypassing the gates simply fails. Policies, reports and training rely on behaviour or detect problems after the fact.

sections.title: Building data unlearning into the pipeline

scenes.title: Designing for forgetting
scenes.sub: Data unlearning capabilities for trained artefacts
scenes.say: Deleting a record from a database takes seconds. Removing its influence from a trained model can take weeks, unless the pipeline was designed for it. | This video covers unlearning as an engineering capability: the workflow, the methods, and the design choices that make forgetting practical.

scenes.title: An unlearning workflow
scenes.say: Unlearning is a workflow, not a single technique. It starts with a trigger: an erasure request, a poisoned dataset, or data that turns out to be unlicensed. | Lineage identifies every affected artefact: datasets, fine-tunes, adapters, retrieval indexes, caches and distilled models. | The data itself is removed from training sets, indexes and caches, so it can’t be used again. | Then each trained artefact is dealt with, using a method chosen by risk. | The result is verified, for example by testing whether the model can still reproduce or reveal the data. | And evidence is recorded: what was removed, how, from which versions, and when.

scenes.title: Unlearning methods
rows: From a checkpoint, without the data
scenes.say: There are three broad families of method. | Retrain from a clean checkpoint without the data. Retrain only the affected shard or adapter. Or adjust the weights directly so the model forgets, which is approximate unlearning. | Retraining gives the highest assurance. Retraining a shard or adapter gives high assurance, if the data really was confined there. Approximate methods give uncertain assurance, so they must be verified. | And the costs run the other way: retraining is the most expensive, partial retraining is moderate, and approximate unlearning is the cheapest.

scenes.title: Design choices that make forgetting practical

items.d: Delete from the index, not the weights
Less to forget in the first place
A deletion queue feeds each cycle

scenes.say: Forgetting is cheap if you plan for it. | Keep personal data in retrieval systems rather than in weights, so deletion from the index is immediate. | Use separate adapters per customer or tenant, so one can be deleted or retrained on its own. | Shard training data, so only one shard needs retraining. | Keep checkpoints and data snapshots, so you can restart from a point before the data arrived. | Minimise and de-identify training data, so there is less to forget in the first place. | And schedule regular retraining, with a deletion queue that feeds each cycle.

items: Unlearning is a workflow: lineage, remove, unlearn, verify, record
Retrain for highest assurance; shards and adapters limit cost
Approximate methods are cheap but must be verified
Design for forgetting: retrieval, adapters, shards, checkpoints
scenes.say: To recap. | Unlearning is a workflow: find affected artefacts through lineage, remove the data, unlearn, verify and record. | Retraining gives the highest assurance, and shards or adapters limit what has to be retrained. | Approximate methods are cheap, but their results must be verified. | And design for forgetting from the start, with retrieval, adapters, sharding and checkpoints.

blocks.md:
### Why unlearning is an engineering capability
Module 3.2 covers the privacy obligations (erasure requests and their limits) and introduces SISA training. Here the focus is on building the capability into MLOps, because triggers for unlearning include more than privacy:
- **Erasure requests** for personal data used in training.
- **Poisoned or corrupted data** discovered after training (Module 3.3).
- **Unlicensed or withdrawn data**, such as content whose licence was revoked or a dataset withdrawn for illegal content (Module 3.7).
- **Hazardous knowledge** a model should not retain.

### Methods
| Method | Description | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Full retraining** | Retrain from scratch, or from a checkpoint taken before the data was added, without the data | Highest assurance; feasible for smaller models or regular retraining cycles |
| **Shard retraining (SISA)** | Data is split into shards, each training a sub-model; retrain only the affected shard | Systems designed for frequent deletion requests |
| **Adapter retraining or removal** | If the data was used only to train an adapter, retrain or delete that adapter | Fine-tuned LLMs with per-task or per-customer adapters |
| **Approximate unlearning** | Techniques such as gradient ascent on the data to forget, or targeted fine-tuning, reduce its influence without full retraining | Large models where retraining is impractical; always verify |
| **Output suppression** | Filters stop the model producing specific information | An interim measure only; the information is still in the weights |

### Verification and its limits
- Test whether the model can still **reproduce, complete or reveal** the forgotten data, using extraction prompts, membership inference tests and canaries planted in the data beforehand (Module 3.3).
- Check that general performance hasn’t degraded too far.
- Research has shown that some approximate methods **hide rather than remove** knowledge, which can resurface after a small amount of further fine-tuning. Benchmarks such as TOFU (forgetting fictitious authors) and WMDP (hazardous knowledge) are used to evaluate methods. Treat approximate unlearning as risk reduction, not proof.

### Building the capability
1. **Lineage** linking data subjects or records to datasets, runs, adapters and deployments (Section 3).
2. **A deletion queue** that removes data from training sets, indexes, caches, logs and backups on schedule.
3. **Architecture for forgetting:** personal data in retrieval rather than weights, adapters per tenant, sharding where requests are frequent, retained checkpoints.
4. **Agreed methods and timelines** per model tier, documented in policy (for example, interim suppression within days, retraining at the next scheduled cycle).
5. **Propagation:** downstream artefacts such as distilled models, merges and synthetic data generated from the original also need handling.
6. **Evidence** of what was done, for regulators and data subjects.

blocks.title: Unlearning questions
blocks.md: Expect the best answer to be **proportionate and verifiable**: remove the data everywhere it is stored now, use interim suppression if needed, and unlearn or retrain on a defined timeline, with evidence. Designs that keep personal data **out of model weights** (retrieval, adapters, de-identification) are usually preferred.

blocks.title: Closed the same day
blocks.md: A recruitment platform fine-tuned a language model on thousands of CVs. A candidate asks for their data to be erased. The team runs an approximate unlearning method against the candidate’s CV, sees that the model no longer answers a direct question about them, and closes the request the same afternoon.

q.q: What is the MAIN weakness of this response?
o: Approximate unlearning methods are never permitted under data protection law
It wasn’t properly verified, so the data may still be recoverable from the model
The request should have been refused, because CVs are public documents anyway
Approximate unlearning also deletes the base model, so the service will fail
q.why: One direct question is not verification: approximate methods can hide rather than remove knowledge. The team should test with extraction and membership inference methods, record evidence, and consider retraining if tests fail.

q.q: A software company fine-tunes one shared model on support tickets from all its business customers. Several customers now require that their data can be removed from any model on request. Which design change BEST supports this?
o: Keep the shared model, and add an output filter that blocks each customer’s company name
Train a separate adapter for each customer, so one can be deleted or retrained on its own
Retrain the shared model from scratch every time any customer asks for removal
Ask customers to remove sensitive details from their tickets before uploading them
q.why: Per-customer adapters confine each customer’s data to an artefact that can be deleted or retrained independently, with high assurance and low cost. Output filters leave the data in the weights, full retraining for every request is costly, and asking customers to sanitise data doesn’t meet the requirement.

o: A training dataset poisoned before it ever reaches the pipeline
Untrusted code running inside a pipeline with the pipeline’s privileges
A pipeline that fails because a dependency has been deleted upstream
A build that produces a corrupted container image entirely by accident
quiz.why: PPE lets an attacker’s code, for example in a pull request, run in the pipeline and use its secrets and access.

quiz.q: Why should CI pipelines use workload identity federation instead of stored cloud keys?
o: Federation makes builds run noticeably faster on shared and self-hosted runners
Short-lived, scoped credentials replace long-lived secrets that can leak
Stored keys can only be used by one pipeline at any one time
Federation removes the need for access control in the cloud
quiz.why: Federated credentials are issued per job, scoped to a repository, branch and environment, and expire quickly.

quiz.q: What does SLSA build level 3 add over level 2?
o: It requires every build to be run manually by two separate engineers
Hardened builds isolated from each other, so provenance can’t be forged
A rule that all artefacts must be stored in a single cloud region
Automatic deployment of every successful build straight to production
quiz.why: Level 3 hardens the build platform, isolating builds and protecting signing material so provenance is trustworthy.

quiz.q: Why should new data land in a quarantine zone before the raw zone?
o: Quarantine storage is much cheaper than raw zone storage
So it can be validated and scanned before anything trusts it
So analysts can edit it before it becomes immutable
Because raw zones can accept new data only once a day
quiz.why: Quarantine holds untrusted data until schema, scanning and hash checks pass, so bad data never enters trusted zones.

quiz.q: Which control BEST preserves evidence of exactly what data arrived in a pipeline?
o: Allowing corrections in place, so that the raw zone always stays accurate
An immutable, versioned raw zone with checksums for each batch
Daily exports of the raw zone to analysts’ laptops for safekeeping
Compressing raw files to keep storage costs as low as possible
quiz.why: Immutability, versioning and checksums preserve the original and make tampering detectable and reversible.

quiz.q: Why tokenise or pseudonymise personal data at ingestion rather than later?
o: Tokens are smaller, which speeds up every later transformation
Later stages, and the people using them, never see raw identifiers
Regulations forbid any processing of identifiers after ingestion
Tokenising at ingestion removes the need for encryption elsewhere
quiz.why: Protecting identifiers at the first opportunity shrinks the number of systems and people exposed to them.

quiz.q: Which detail is MOST important to record about the base model in fine-tuning lineage?
o: Its marketing name, as shown on the provider’s website
Its exact version identifier and its content hash
The number of downloads it has on the model hub
The date on which the model was first announced
quiz.why: Only an exact version and hash identify precisely which weights the fine-tune was built on.

quiz.q: Why should lineage be captured automatically by the pipeline?
o: Automatic records take up less storage than manual ones
Manual records develop gaps and errors; automatic capture is complete
Regulators accept only lineage that was generated automatically by a pipeline
Automatic capture removes the need for a model registry
quiz.why: Lineage is only useful if it is complete and accurate, which manual records rarely are over time.

quiz.q: What makes a pipeline gate enforceable rather than advisory?
o: A dashboard showing how many builds passed each gate last month
Signed gate attestations that deployment verifies before accepting artefacts
An email to the whole team whenever any gate in the pipeline fails
A policy document listing every gate in the pipeline in detail, signed by management
quiz.why: If deployment refuses artefacts without valid attestations, gates can’t be skipped by going around the pipeline.

quiz.q: Why should evaluation thresholds be agreed before a model is tested?
o: So that the model can be trained to hit the thresholds directly
So they can’t be relaxed after a failure to let a release through
Because evaluation tools can’t run until thresholds are configured
So the thresholds can be published to customers in advance
quiz.why: Thresholds set after seeing results invite moving the goalposts; pre-agreed thresholds keep the gate honest.

quiz.q: Which unlearning method gives the HIGHEST assurance that data has been forgotten?
o: Output suppression filters
Retraining without the data
Approximate gradient-based unlearning
Lowering the sampling temperature
quiz.why: A model retrained without the data never learned from it. Suppression hides outputs, and approximate methods may leave traces.

quiz.q: Why must approximate unlearning be verified?
o: It always deletes the model’s training logs as a side effect
Some methods hide rather than remove knowledge, which can resurface
Regulators always require proof in the form of a complete retrain from scratch
It changes the licence terms that apply to the model
quiz.why: Research shows some approximate methods merely suppress knowledge, which can return after further fine-tuning, so test for extraction and leakage.

exam.q: A model-serving image is built from a large GPU base image tagged “latest”, with dependencies installed without version pins. A scan finds 300 vulnerabilities, and the image differs on every rebuild. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Run the vulnerability scanner more often, so that new issues are found sooner
A minimal base pinned by digest, dependencies pinned by hash, and a signed SBOM
Accept the vulnerabilities, because GPU images are always large and complex
Rebuild the image every hour, so that it always has the newest packages
exam.why: Minimal, pinned inputs cut the attack surface and make builds reproducible and verifiable; an SBOM and signature make the result auditable. More scanning finds problems without fixing them, and unpinned rebuilds keep changing what is shipped.

exam.q: A team stores a long-lived cloud access key with production deployment rights in its CI system’s settings. Which change BEST reduces the risk?
o: Rotate the key every 90 days, and restrict who can view or change the CI system’s settings
Use federated, short-lived credentials scoped to the protected branch and environment
Encrypt the key using the CI system’s own built-in secret store feature
Move the key into the repository, so that any changes to it are reviewed
exam.why: Federation removes the standing secret altogether, and scoping limits use to reviewed code deploying to the intended environment. Rotation and encryption still leave a powerful long-lived key; a key in a repository is worse.

exam.q: A fraud model’s training data comes from a transformation job that analysts sometimes edit directly in production to fix urgent issues. An auditor asks how the organisation knows the training data hasn’t been tampered with. What is the BEST response?
o: Show the auditor the job’s current code, which has now been corrected and fully tested
Move transformations to reviewed, versioned code, with immutable data and audit logs
Ask the analysts to keep a written log of any manual changes they make
Restrict manual edits in production to the most senior analysts only
exam.why: Reviewed, versioned transformation code deployed by the pipeline, with immutable data and audit logs, makes the training data reproducible and tampering detectable. Current code says nothing about past runs, and manual logs or seniority don’t make edits controlled.

exam.q: A regulator asks a bank which data and base model built the credit model deployed last March, and to reproduce it. Records were kept in spreadsheets and some are missing. What should the bank implement to avoid this in future?
o: A rule that the shared spreadsheets must be updated within one week of every training run
Automatic lineage linking base model, data snapshots, code, runs and deployments
A policy of retraining every model from scratch at the start of each month
Keeping every model the bank has ever trained in production permanently
exam.why: Automatic, linked lineage records exactly what each deployed model was built from, so it can be explained and reproduced. Spreadsheet rules still rely on people, and retraining or keeping old models doesn’t answer the question.

exam.q: A pipeline has a “skip evaluation” flag that engineers can set themselves. It was used in 40% of releases last quarter. What is the BEST corrective action?
o: Remove the flag, and rely on engineers’ own judgement about releases instead
Replace it with break-glass: independent approval, time limits, logging and review
Keep the flag, but report each use of it to management every quarter
Speed up the evaluations, so that engineers no longer feel any need to skip them at all
exam.why: Emergencies need a route, but it must be controlled: independent approval, expiry, logging and review afterwards. Self-service skipping isn’t a control, quarterly reports are too late, and faster evaluations help but don’t enforce anything.

exam.q: A health app fine-tuned an LLM on patient messages. A patient requests erasure, and lineage shows their data was used in one fine-tuning run. Retraining takes three weeks. What is the BEST approach?
o: Refuse the request, because data held in model weights can’t ever be removed
Delete the data everywhere now, suppress meanwhile, then retrain or unlearn and verify
Apply output suppression permanently, and then close the request as complete
Retrain immediately, and take the whole service offline until the retraining has finished
exam.why: A proportionate response removes the data from all stores at once, limits exposure with interim suppression, and removes its influence on a defined timeline with verification and evidence. Refusal and permanent suppression leave the data in the weights, and halting the service is disproportionate.

exam.q: An organisation wants to offer customers a private assistant that learns from each customer’s documents, with guaranteed removal when a customer leaves. Which architecture BEST supports this?
o: Fine-tune one shared model on all customers’ documents, for the best quality
Per-customer retrieval indexes, with per-customer adapters only where tuning is needed
Train a new base model each year from all customers’ data combined together
Place each customer’s documents in the system prompt of every chat session that they start
exam.why: Keeping customer knowledge in per-customer indexes, and any tuning in per-customer adapters, makes removal a matter of deleting those artefacts. A shared model mixes everyone’s data into the same weights.
